Introduction:
**1:** Both sections make the same core argument with strikingly close rhetorical devices: the expected section's "common trap" of black-box thinking and "this is not real engineering" line are matched almost point for point by this version's "treats the LLM as a black box" and "That is not engineering. It is gambling." This version also adds a first-person aside ("I have too") that reads as the personal-story framing the guideline's Narrative Flow describes, closer to that instruction's spirit than any other article graded so far, though per the standing ruling that isn't what earns the score - the substantive hook match is what does.

The Challenge with Complex Single LLM Calls:
**1:** Both sections cover the same core problems (debugging difficulty, inability to update one part without breaking others, lost-in-the-middle, accuracy decreasing with complexity) and the same practical example end-to-end, including full FAQ/FAQList Pydantic classes. The added Stanford/UC Berkeley attribution for the lost-in-the-middle research is accurate (verified against the cited exploitation-phase source, which names Stanford, UC Berkeley, and Samaya AI) and additive.

The Power of Modularity: Why Chain LLM Calls?:
**1:** Both sections cover the same chaining definition and the same four benefits (modularity, accuracy, debugging, flexibility) and downsides (latency, cost, information loss).

Building a Sequential Workflow: FAQ Generation Pipeline:
**1:** Both sections cover the same 3-step chain (with matching bolded step labels in the overview list), the same three functions and class names, combining them into sequential_workflow, and the same measured 22.20-second execution time.

Optimizing Sequential Workflows With Parallel Processing:
**1:** Both sections cover the same core moves: independent per-question work run concurrently, asyncio for I/O-bound operations, the same 8.98-second result, and the sequential-vs-parallel trade-off including rate limits/backoff.

Introducing Dynamic Behavior: Routing and Conditional Logic:
**0:** Both sections cover the need for routing, LLM-as-classifier/dispatcher, and divide-and-conquer. However, as in four of the six other articles graded, this section never mentions the billing-vs-technical-support example the expected section uses here specifically to preview Sections 6-7 - a missing substantive idea the guideline's own bullet list explicitly requests.

Building a Basic Routing Workflow:
**0:** Both sections cover classify_intent, the per-intent prompts, and handle_query with routing logic. BORDERLINE, different in kind from every other article graded: this version's closing paragraph explicitly states that a billing query is also correctly routed to the billing handler ("while a query about an invoice is routed to the billing handler"), so the router's generalization across intent types IS acknowledged, unlike the other six articles which don't mention a second intent type at all. However, the expected section actually demonstrates this with a second worked code example (classify_intent + handle_query called again on a billing query, with shown output), and this version only asserts the outcome in prose without a second code execution. I scored this 0, treating a demonstrated example as categorically different from an asserted one, but this is the closest call on this recurring issue across every article so far and a stricter or looser reading could go either way.

Orchestrator-Worker Pattern: Dynamic Task Decomposition:
**1:** Both sections cover the orchestrator decomposing the query into typed tasks, dispatching to workers, and a synthesizer combining results. The added production-limitations content (context window bottleneck, model-tiering, synthesizer failure modes - see depth_enhancement) is additive.

Conclusion:
**1:** Both sections recap the same four patterns and both preview future lessons by substance (tools and reasoning), with this version also referencing memory as a bonus beyond the expected section's own two references.
